steps.title: A query inside a query
steps.content: A subquery is a SELECT placed inside another SQL statement. It can return one value, one column or a set of rows, depending on its use.
steps.example: SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee);

steps.title: Use IN for a set
steps.prompt: What does WHERE department_id IN (10, 20) select?
options: Only rows with both departments at once
steps.explanation: IN matches a value against any value in the supplied list or subquery result.

steps.title: Understand EXISTS
steps.content: EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. It is often used with a correlated subquery that references a row from the outer query.
steps.example: SELECT d.name FROM Department d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Employee e WHERE e.department_id=d.id);
steps.tip: EXISTS tests whether a matching row exists; it does not return the matching rows themselves.

steps.title: Choose the existence test
steps.prompt: Which operator is designed to test whether a subquery returns at least one row?
steps.explanation: EXISTS evaluates to true when the subquery returns one or more rows.

steps.title: Correlated and non-correlated subqueries
steps.content: A non-correlated subquery can run independently of the outer query. A correlated subquery refers to an outer-query column and is logically evaluated for each candidate outer row, though the optimizer may transform it.
steps.example: A correlated EXISTS can check whether each department has at least one employee.
